1051.title: The lotus leaf
1051.hook: a lotus leaf sits in the pond all day, and the water rolls off it in beads
1051.carry: act fully, cling to nothing, like the lotus leaf
1051.howItsDone: The paths of karma, bhakti and jnana are walked side by side and in combination: selfless work and service, devotion in worship and kirtan, and study and inquiry with a teacher; the Gita is read as holding all three.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the modern teachers, and Ramana's question: to whom did this thought come? Today, the three tracks.

Rain falls on a pond. The water gathers on a lotus leaf in bright beads, rolls to the edge, and slides off. The leaf has been in the water all its life. It isn't wet. In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna wants to put down his bow and walk away from the battle. Krishna doesn't tell him to leave the pond. In the fifth chapter he gives him that leaf, a picture of someone who acts fully in the world and isn't stained by it. This year the path read it on three tracks: karma, bhakti and jnana.
screen: `WATER ON A LOTUS LEAF.` → `ARJUNA WANTS TO WALK AWAY.` → `STAY IN THE POND, NOT WET.`

segments.voice: Here is the Gita's line, in paraphrase: one who acts while placing every action in Brahman, letting go of clinging, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not touched by water. Hold that leaf up to each of the year's three tracks. The karma track read Gita chapters three, four and five, and designed a year of service. There the leaf means doing the work well and setting down the result. The bhakti track read the Gita Govinda and the Bhagavata's tenth book, and sang kirtan. There the leaf turns into an offering. Elsewhere the Gita has Krishna say, in paraphrase: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me. The act is the same. Now it is a gift. The jnana track read Shankara's Crest-Jewel of Discrimination and the Ashtavakra Gita. There the leaf is the witness. Ashtavakra tells King Janaka, in paraphrase: you are not earth, water, fire, air or space; know yourself as the witness of all these. Three tracks, three readings of one leaf. And the Gita itself, in the same chapter, says that only the childish call the path of knowledge and the path of action different; the one who truly stands in either reaches the fruit of both. Read that way, the tracks aren't a contest. They're three ways up, and under all three sits one teaching: freedom doesn't mean leaving the world. Stay in the water, do your dharma fully, and let go of clinging.
screen: `NOT TOUCHED, LIKE A LOTUS LEAF.` · `KARMA: SET DOWN THE RESULT.` · `BHAKTI: MAKE IT AN OFFERING.` · `JNANA: THE WITNESS, NEVER WET.` · then, large: `STAY IN THE WATER. LET GO OF CLINGING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary task from today, a dish, an email, a drive, and hold it for a few breaths the karma way: done well, the result let go. Then the bhakti way: if you pray, see it as something offered. Then the jnana way: notice the one who watches it being done, still and dry like the leaf, and don't pick a favorite.
Padma-patra. The lotus leaf, sitting in water all its life and never wet, the Gita's picture for the three tracks of karma, bhakti and jnana.
Your line: act fully, cling to nothing, like the lotus leaf. Krishna didn't send Arjuna out of the pond. Tomorrow, a boy and a mantra. See you tomorrow.

1052.title: Dhruva's mantra
1052.hook: a little prince is pulled off his father's lap, and walks into the forest with one mantra
1052.carry: sadhana is the practice you keep returning to
1052.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a daily sadhana, often japa: a mantra from a teacher or the family, repeated on a mala of 108 beads at about the same time each day. Dhruva's story is told to children as a picture of steady devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, padma-patra: Krishna's lotus leaf, in the water and never wet. Today, the practices, and a boy who kept one.
screen: `THE LOTUS LEAF.` · `IN THE WATER, NEVER WET.`

segments.voice: A little prince named Dhruva climbs onto his father's lap. His stepmother, the king's favorite queen, pulls him off. Only her own son belongs there, she says; if Dhruva wants that seat, he should pray to the Lord to be born again as her son. The king says nothing. Dhruva runs to his own mother, Suniti, in tears. She tells him the only one who can truly help is the Lord, Vishnu. So the boy walks out toward the forest. The Bhagavata Purana tells it, and Hindu children still hear it.
screen: `PULLED OFF HIS FATHER'S LAP.` → `ONLY THE LORD CAN HELP.` → `A BOY WALKS INTO THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: On the way, the sage Narada meets him and tries to turn him back: you're only a child, this is too hard. Dhruva won't go home. So Narada gives him what a teacher gives: a place, the forest of Madhuvana by the Yamuna, and a mantra. Om namo bhagavate vasudevaya: I bow to the Lord. Dhruva repeats it day after day. In the telling he eats less and less, fruit, then leaves, then only water, then air, until his practice weighs on the whole universe, and Vishnu comes to stand in front of him. And here's the turn the story is loved for. The boy had come for a throne. Vishnu grants it, but on the walk home, having seen the Lord, Dhruva is sorry, the story says, that he asked for so small a thing. He does rule, later, and at the end he's given a place in the sky that never moves: the pole star, still called Dhruva. The tradition's word for what he did is sadhana: a spiritual practice kept up until it becomes yours. Very often it's japa, a mantra from a teacher or the family, repeated on a mala of a hundred and eight beads, every day. The Yoga Sutra says what makes practice hold, in paraphrase: a long time, without breaks, and with care. Most of us won't live on air in a forest. But the same fingers coming back to the same beads is Dhruva's road, sized for a life.
screen: `NARADA GIVES HIM A MANTRA.` · `DAY AFTER DAY, IN THE FOREST.` · `SORRY HE ASKED FOR SO LITTLE.` · `THE POLE STAR, AND SADHANA.` · then, large: `THE PRACTICE YOU KEEP RETURNING TO.`

segments.voice: If you have a mala, hold it in your right hand; if not, count on your fingers. Say a mantra softly, once per bead or finger: Dhruva's, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, or om namah shivaya, or the name of God your family uses. If you don't pray, repeat one slow word, like peace. Don't count for a score. When the mind wanders, simply go on to the next bead, the way Dhruva went on to the next day.
Sadhana. A spiritual practice kept up until it becomes yours, like the mantra Dhruva repeated in the forest until the Lord came.
Your line: sadhana is the practice you keep returning to. Dhruva's star still doesn't move. Tomorrow, how the Gita ends. Until tomorrow.

1053.title: Sanjaya remembers
1053.hook: at the end of the Gita, the charioteer who heard it all keeps remembering it, and rejoices again and again
1053.carry: reciting the gita again is itself worship
1053.howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Bhagavad Gita again and again, a chapter a day or the whole of it on Gita Jayanti, since the Gita itself calls studying it worship; the epics and Puranas are counted among the smriti, the remembered texts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sadhana: Dhruva's mantra, kept day after day until the Lord came. Today the week of summit sits closes.

The Bhagavad Gita doesn't end with Krishna's last word. It ends with two people remembering. Arjuna speaks once more, briefly, and then the voice goes back to Sanjaya, the king's charioteer, who has been describing the whole conversation from far away. Sanjaya says that as he remembers this dialogue, he rejoices, again and again. And as he remembers that form of Krishna, he is amazed, and rejoices again. A fitting close for a week of summit sits.
screen: `THE GITA ENDS IN MEMORY.` → `SANJAYA REMEMBERS.` → `AND REJOICES, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Arjuna says near the close of the eighteenth chapter, in paraphrase: my confusion is gone. Through your grace I have regained memory. I stand firm, my doubts are scattered. I will do as you say. He doesn't say he has learned something new. He says memory has come back. The word there is smriti, memory, and it carries weight in this tradition. It's also the name for the great body of remembered texts, the epics and the Puranas among them. And just before that, Krishna says something about this very conversation. In paraphrase: whoever studies this dialogue of ours worships me with the offering of knowledge, and whoever simply hears it with faith, without scoffing, is freed too. That's the teaching, and it's why Hindu families and temples recite the Gita again and again: a chapter a day, the whole of it on Gita Jayanti, the same eighteen chapters for a lifetime. In this tradition, going back over sacred words isn't review. It's worship. So look at this week from the top: a king who wouldn't leave a dog, a mother who saw the universe in her son's mouth, the saints singing at home, Ramana's question, a lotus leaf, a boy with one mantra. None of it was new. All of it was remembered. And Sanjaya shows the last step. He doesn't remember once. He keeps returning, and keeps being glad.
screen: `I HAVE REGAINED MEMORY.` · `SMRITI: THE REMEMBERED TEXTS.` · `TO STUDY IT IS WORSHIP.` · `RETURN, AND REJOICE AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WAY, AS ONE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Let the week walk back through you, one picture for each sit: a dog on a mountain road, a child's open mouth, a weaver singing at a loom, a question, water rolling off a leaf, a boy in the forest with one mantra. Give each one a breath, then let them go and sit with whatever stays. If one of them makes you glad, let yourself be glad again, the way Sanjaya was.
Smriti. Memory, the word Arjuna uses when his confusion clears, and the name for the remembered texts, including the epics.
Your line: reciting the Gita again is itself worship. Sanjaya rejoiced every time. Tomorrow, a goddess made of light. See you then.

1054.title: Every god's light
1054.hook: beaten gods pour out their light, and the light becomes a goddess
1054.carry: shakti is god's power, worshipped as the mother
1054.howItsDone: The Devi Mahatmya is recited in homes and temples, especially during Navaratri, the goddess's festival; the scene of her forming from the gods' light is painted, sung and acted out.

segments.voice: Last week ended on smriti: Sanjaya remembering the Gita and rejoicing, again and again. A new week, the last of the year, and this one looks forward.

The gods have lost. A buffalo demon, Mahisha, has driven them out of heaven. Led by Brahma, they go to Shiva and Vishnu and tell them everything. And the three great gods, hearing it, grow so angry that light begins to pour out of their faces. Year three on this path was the great story and the saints. Year four is the schools and the goddess, and that scene is its first ridge.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE LOST.` → `LIGHT POURS FROM THEIR FACES.` → `THE SCHOOLS AND THE GODDESS.`

segments.voice: That scene is from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess. In its second episode, in paraphrase, a great blaze of light streams from Vishnu, from Shiva, from Brahma, and then from all the other gods as well. The light gathers into one mass, like a burning mountain filling the sky. And the mass takes form as a woman. Then each god gives her something of his own. Shiva draws a trident out of his trident and hands it to her. Vishnu brings forth a discus from his discus. One by one, the others give. She laughs, and the world shakes, and she goes out to meet Mahisha. Look at what the story is saying in its own way. The goddess isn't presented as a helper sent by one god. She's what appears when every power is gathered into one, and she can act when the gods themselves couldn't. The tradition's word for that power is shakti. And here's the teaching. For many Hindus, God's power to act is feminine, and is worshipped as the Mother: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati and Parvati, read as faces of one Devi. That's why, at Navaratri, the nine nights of the goddess, families and temples chant this very text and honor her night after night. Later in the same book, the gods praise her as the goddess who lives in all beings as power, and bow to her, again and again. Year four opens with her: the Devi Mahatmya read whole, and Navaratri as a curriculum. This week looks at the ranges beyond her from here, just to know their shape.
screen: `THE GLORY OF THE GODDESS.` · `EVERY GOD'S LIGHT, GATHERED INTO ONE.` · `EACH GOD GIVES A WEAPON.` · `SHAKTI: GOD'S POWER, WORSHIPPED AS MOTHER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST RIDGE OF YEAR FOUR.`

If you don't pray, picture the people in your day and bow to the strength in each.
Shakti. Power, energy, and a name for the goddess herself, made when every god's light gathered into one.

1055.title: The hunter's night
1055.hook: a hungry hunter waits all night in a tree, and the leaves he drops land somewhere he can't see
1055.carry: shiva accepts even a vigil kept without knowing
1055.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, devotees fast, keep vigil through the night, chant to Shiva, and offer water, milk and bilva leaves on the Shiva linga, and the story of the hunter is often retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shakti: the goddess, made of every god's light gathered into one, the first ridge of year four. Today, the next ridge.

A hunter has caught nothing all day, and his family is waiting for food. Night comes. He climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and settles in with his bow. He's cold. He's hungry. He can't let himself sleep. So his hands stay busy: he plucks leaves from the branches and lets them fall, one after another, into the dark below. He has no idea what's down there. The story is told in the Shiva Purana, and retold on one particular night of the year.
screen: `A HUNTER, EMPTY-HANDED.` → `ALL NIGHT IN A TREE.` → `LEAVES FALLING IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here is the turn, in paraphrase. The tree is a bilva tree, whose leaves are offered to Shiva. And at its foot, unseen in the dark, stands a Shiva linga. All night long, the hunter's restless leaves fall onto it, along with drops of water. He stays awake through every watch of the night. It is Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, though he doesn't know it. When deer come to the water, he draws his bow, and each time he ends up letting them go. By morning, the story says, his heart has changed, and Shiva appears to him. He fasted because he had no food. He kept vigil because he was afraid to sleep. He worshipped because his hands were fidgeting. The story is gentle about it. Shiva accepted the night anyway. And that's why Maha Shivaratri is kept the way it is. Hindus do on purpose what the hunter did by accident: they fast, stay awake through the watches of the night, pour water on the linga, offer bilva leaves, and often tell his story. It's also why Shiva has a loving nickname, Bholenath, the simple, easily pleased lord. The rites matter, and people keep them with care. But the story teaches that Shiva's grace runs ahead of our understanding: a night turned toward him counts, even half-understood. That's the second range in year four. After the goddess comes Shiva: the Shiva Purana in selections, Nataraja the dancer, the Rudram, a first look at Kashmir Shaivism, and Maha Shivaratri itself, taught watch by watch, the way the hunter kept it without meaning to.
screen: `A BILVA TREE, A HIDDEN LINGA.` · `A VIGIL KEPT WITHOUT KNOWING.` · `WHY SHIVARATRI IS KEPT THIS WAY.` · `BHOLENATH: EASILY PLEASED.` · then, large: `THE SECOND RIDGE: SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, as if this were a short watch of the night. Each time you breathe out, picture one leaf leaving your hand and falling into the dark, onto something you can't see, without needing to know where it lands. If you're tired, that's fine; the hunter was too.
Bilva. The tree whose leaves fell, by accident, on a hidden Shiva linga all through the night, the night a hunter kept without knowing it was holy.
Your line: Shiva accepts even a vigil kept without knowing. The hunter never saw where his leaves fell. See you tomorrow.

1056.title: The lord white as jasmine
1056.hook: a queen's question goes unanswered in a hall of men, and a poet leaves a palace to sing to Shiva in her own words
1056.carry: in bhakti, anyone can speak to god in their own words
1056.howItsDone: Akka Mahadevi's vachanas are sung and recited in Karnataka and Lal Ded's sayings are quoted in Kashmir; across India, Hindus pray and sing bhajans to God in their own languages, as the bhakti saints did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bilva tree, and a hunter who kept Shiva's holy night without knowing it. Today, another ridge.
screen: `THE RANGES AHEAD.` · `A NIGHT KEPT WITHOUT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: This year, in the dice game, Draupadi was dragged into a hall full of men and asked them a question. Had her husband lost himself before he staked her? If he had, was she his to lose? Bhishma answered that the way of dharma was too subtle for him to decide. Young Vikarna spoke up for her and was shouted down. Draupadi's voice reaches us inside a vast story told about her. But some women in this tradition left their own words behind, and one of them walked out of a palace to do it.
screen: `DRAUPADI'S QUESTION.` → `THE ELDERS CAN'T SETTLE IT.` → `A WOMAN, IN HER OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Akka Mahadevi lived in Karnataka in the twelfth century. The story told about her says a king wanted her, and she wanted only Shiva. She left the palace and, the story says, walked out into the world covered only by her own long hair, looking for her lord. She found her way to a circle of Shiva's devotees, poets like Basavanna and Allama Prabhu, who sang short free poems called vachanas, sayings, in Kannada, the language people spoke at home. Akka's vachanas speak to one beloved, her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna, the lord white as jasmine. Some readers hear them as blunt and tender at once: a woman telling God, plainly, that she will have no other. That's the heart of bhakti, the path of loving devotion, and one of Hinduism's great turns. God can be loved directly, as your own, and spoken to in your own language, by anyone: a queen or a weaver, a man or a woman. It's why Hindu devotion lives in Tamil and Hindi, Kannada and Gujarati, not only in Sanskrit, and why grandmothers sing to God in the words they grew up with. Far to the north, Lal Ded, also called Lalla, did the same in Kashmiri. In one saying attributed to her, in paraphrase, she wandered far, searching, and found what she was looking for at home, inside. Year four sets these voices beside the women of the epics, not as a special topic, but as part of the main road.
screen: `AKKA LEAVES THE PALACE.` · `VACHANAS, IN KANNADA.` · `THE LORD WHITE AS JASMINE.` · `BHAKTI: GOD, IN YOUR OWN WORDS.` · then, large: `PART OF THE MAIN ROAD.`

segments.voice: Speak to God, or to whatever you hold highest, in the language you think in at home, not the one you'd use to impress anyone. One or two plain sentences, the way Akka spoke to her lord white as jasmine. If you don't pray, say them to the day ahead. Then sit for a few breaths and let the words settle, without fixing them.
Vachana. A saying: the short free poems Akka Mahadevi sang to Shiva in Kannada, her own language, the way bhakti speaks to God.
Your line: in bhakti, anyone can speak to God in their own words. Akka did, in Kannada. Tomorrow, one more ridge. Rest well.

1057.title: Who truly knows?
1057.hook: the oldest Hindu scripture tells how everything began, then asks who really knows
1057.carry: in the vedas, honest questioning is itself sacred
1057.howItsDone: Hymns of the Rig Veda are still chanted by memory in traditional recitation, passed from teacher to student, and the Nasadiya Sukta is often cited, by Hindus and others, as a sign that Hindu scripture makes room for open questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vachana, the short free poems Akka Mahadevi sang to Shiva, and the women of the tradition, like Lal Ded, heard in their own words.
screen: `VACHANA: FREE POEMS TO SHIVA.` · `WOMEN, IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Before there was anything, a hymn in the Rig Veda says, there was neither what is nor what is not. No air, and no sky beyond it. No death, and no deathlessness, no sign of night or day. Only the One, breathing without wind, by its own power. Darkness, hidden in darkness. Then, by the power of heat, the One came to be. Desire came, the first seed of mind, and the sages, searching in their hearts, found the bond between what is and what is not. That's the creation story of the Nasadiya Sukta, chanted for around three thousand years. And then it does something you might not expect from scripture.
screen: `NEITHER WHAT IS NOR WHAT IS NOT.` → `THE ONE, BREATHING WITHOUT WIND.` → `DARKNESS, HIDDEN IN DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: It asks. Who truly knows? Who here could say where this creation came from? Even the gods, it says, came later than this making, so who knows where it arose? Then the last line. The one who watches over it all from the highest heaven surely knows. Or perhaps that one does not know. Here's what that shows about this religion. The Vedas are shruti, what was heard: Hinduism's oldest and most sacred texts, passed from teacher to student by memory, syllable by syllable, and still chanted that way. And right inside them sits an honest question, kept as carefully as any prayer. Hindu scripture holds more than one account of creation: a cosmic person in one hymn, a golden womb in another, and this one, which leaves the answer open. Asking, in this tradition, is part of the path, not a threat to it. Centuries later the Brahma Sutra would open with the words: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Next year the path climbs into the Vedas themselves: hymns to Agni, the fire, to Ushas, the dawn, and this one. And today? When a child looks up at the stars and asks where it all came from, a Hindu parent can tell the old stories and also say: our oldest hymn asked that too, and left room for you to keep asking. Faith here doesn't mean pretending to know.
screen: `WHO TRULY KNOWS?` · `OR PERHAPS THAT ONE DOES NOT KNOW.` · `SHRUTI: KEPT BY HEART.` · `NOW, THE INQUIRY INTO BRAHMAN.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION IS SACRED TOO.`

segments.voice: Settle, and quietly ask the hymn's question: before all this, what was there? Don't reach for an answer; let the question stay in you, the way the sages searched in their hearts. When the mind hurries to fill it, come back to the breath, which arrived before you asked for it. If you pray, rest before God, or the gods, with the question still open; if you don't, simply sit beside it.
Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation, the Rig Veda hymn that asks who really knows, and ends: or perhaps not.
Your line: in the Vedas, honest questioning is itself sacred. The oldest hymns kept a question as carefully as a prayer. See you tomorrow.
